title: Self-reliance, carefully
hookLine: self-trust can slide into selfishness; Emerson also wrote of the one soul in all

cards: A good man, Emerson writes, came to him that very day to remind him of his duty to help the poor. Emerson, in Self-Reliance, snaps back: "Are they my poor?"

He grudges, he says, what he gives to people who don't belong to him. He admits he sometimes gives the dollar anyway, and then calls it a wicked dollar he'll one day have the backbone to keep. It's a jolt.
After trust thyself and insist on yourself, here is where that road can lead if you follow it carelessly. So today, read slowly.

teach.h: ARE THEY MY POOR? THE HARD EDGE.
teach.b: First, the hard edge, honestly. Self-Reliance has passages like that one, where self-trust sounds a lot like turning your back on people.
It's possible to quote Emerson to excuse exactly that: my path, my rules, not my problem. It's in the text, and it's fair to say so.
Fairness also means adding what comes right after: for the people he feels bound to, Emerson says, he would go to prison if need be. Second, Emerson's own question.
A little later he stops and asks who, exactly, is being trusted.
Who is the trustee? Not the little self that wants its own way. He calls it the original Self, the source he names Instinct, or Intuition.
And then: "We lie in the lap of immense intelligence." The self he trusts is not a private island. It's a door into something everyone shares.
Third, where that leads. In other essays, Emerson writes of one soul in all people, a single life each of us is part of; that gets its own day soon.
If the self you trust opens onto what everyone shares, trusting it can't simply mean ignoring them. Fourth, the balance. Self-trust says: don't hand your judgment to the crowd.
Care says: the crowd is made of people, each with the same deep self.
A self-reliance that forgets others shrinks to selfishness.
A kindness that never trusts itself shrinks to people-pleasing. Read carefully, Emerson asks for the harder thing: someone who stands on their own feet and still turns toward the people around them.

how: Some readers of Self-Reliance weigh its hard passages, like 'are they my poor?', against Emerson's own account of the deeper self being trusted, one he says opens onto an intelligence everyone shares.

o: looking after yourself first and others only later
trusting a deep self that opens onto everyone else
giving away everything you own to strangers

s: Self-Reliance has no passages that sound selfish
it does: 'are they my poor?' is in the same essay.
Emerson asks who, exactly, is being trusted
his answer is the original Self, which he calls Instinct or Intuition.
the self Emerson trusts is a private island

games.q: you've just read 'trust thyself' and 'are they my poor?' a friend needs help. what does a careful reading of Emerson point to?
o: it's not my problem; trust thyself.
drop my own judgment and do whatever they ask.
trust my judgment and care for them together.
games.why: Emerson asks who the trustee is, and answers with a self that opens onto what everyone shares, so self-trust and care belong together.

practice: Bring to mind one decision in front of you and ask what your own honest judgment says, apart from what anyone expects. Then picture the people it touches, one face at a time, and ask what care for them would add.
You're not giving up your judgment or ignoring them; you're looking for the choice that holds both.

wordCard.voice: Self-reliance. Emerson's word, read carefully: trusting a self that opens onto what everyone shares, which means trusting yourself and caring for others together. Today's word.

carryVoice: Your line: self and others. The trustee, in Emerson's picture, is no private island. See you tomorrow.
